base_s1.explanation: The unit responds mainly to circular dials and faces with radial tick marks or numerals, such as watch faces, compasses, clocks, gauges and speedometers. It responds more weakly to other round, rimmed or curved-arc shapes like bowls, plaques, round shields, mirrors, arches and curved railings.

parsed.evidence: Most top activations (8–10) are watches, compasses, clocks, a multimeter dial and a speedometer, with the box usually on the dial's rim or ticks. parsed.missing_data: Activations on round objects that have no tick marks (plates, wheels, coins) and on non-round objects that do have ticks (rulers) would show whether the unit cares about the circular rim or the dial markings.

P_s1.explanation: The unit responds mainly to the curved rim of round dial faces such as watches, compasses, gauges, speedometers and clock faces, with the peak often at the upper edge where the bezel meets the tick marks. It responds more weakly to other circular or arched contours such as a bridge arch, a bowl rim, a round plaque, a rainbow-arc sign and a curved railing.

It responds more weakly to other circular or arched contours such as a bridge arch, a bowl rim, a round plaque, a rainbow-arc sign and a curved railing.
parsed.evidence: Most of the top 20 are watches, compasses and gauges (#1-3, 5, 7, 9-11, 15-17), and the rest are mostly arcs or rims (#6, 8, 12, 13, 18-20); random photos without such structure score only 1-4. The unit is unusually sensitive to phase scrambling (percentile 4) and patch shuffling (percentile 9), and it keeps most of its activation in edge maps, which fits a shape or contour feature rather than colour or texture.
parsed.missing_data: Activations on synthetic stimuli (plain circles and arcs of varying curvature, with and without tick marks) would show whether dial markings matter beyond the curvature itself.
